ACROSS ALL FIVE PAGES

Which block for which operation

Pick an operation to see the area to cover and the block options.

OPERATION
Carotid endarterectomy (awake)
Thyroid or parathyroid surgery
Clavicle fracture fixation
Craniotomy, head pins or awake craniotomy
Posterior craniotomy or VP shunt
Forehead or frontal scalp surgery
Cleft lip repair (child)
Cleft palate repair (child)
Lower lip or chin surgery
Awake tracheal intubation
Cataract surgery
Vitreoretinal or other long eye surgery

Carotid endarterectomy (awake)

Front

Right side

Dense: reliable
Moderate: usually adequate
One side shown (the patient’s right). Areas are schematic: nerve territories vary and overlap.
Great auricular (C2–C3): angle of the jaw, over the parotid, most of the ear
Transverse cervical (C2–C3): the front of the neck
Lesser occipital (C2): the scalp behind and above the ear
Supraclavicular (C3–C4): lower neck, over the clavicle, top of the shoulder and upper chest
AREA TO COVER
C2–C4 skin of the neck on the operated side, plus deep infiltration by the surgeon
Block options
FIRST CHOICE
Superficial or intermediate cervical plexus block, with the surgeon’s infiltration
Open superficial and intermediate cervical plexus on the cervical plexus page
→
NOT RECOMMENDED
Deep cervical plexus block

More serious complications and more conversions to general anaesthesia, without a better block for this operation.

Open deep cervical plexus on the cervical plexus page
→
Practical notes
The awake patient is the neurological monitor while the carotid is clamped.
Local and general anaesthesia had the same 30-day outcomes in the GALA trial: choose by the patient and the team.
Plan how you would convert to general anaesthesia with the head under the drapes.

Local anaesthetic systemic toxicity. Arteries in the head and neck run straight to the brain: 0.5 ml or less injected into one can cause a seizure. Aspirate, inject slowly, and keep the total within the maximum, especially with bilateral blocks and topical lidocaine.
